analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to all earnings and uses an elderly-focused inflation index for benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would phase out the payroll tax cap above $176,100 and switch Social Security's inflation adjustment to a seniors-specific index, has been referred to three House committees with no action since its August 12, 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, wages above about $176,100 a year are exempt from Social Security taxes. This bill would phase out that exemption over six years, so that after 2031 every dollar of earnings is taxed, and it would credit some of those previously untaxed earnings toward slightly higher benefits for high earners. It would also switch the annual cost-of-living adjustment to an index reflecting the spending of people over 62, which typically rises faster, and shield any resulting benefit increase from counting as income for Medicaid or SSI eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, especially lower- and middle-income seniors, would get more accurate inflation adjustments and stronger program financing; high earners who currently stop paying Social Security tax at the cap would pay more.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Phases out the taxable maximum between 2026 and 2031 so that after 2031 all earnings are subject to the Social Security payroll tax, which extends the program's financing base [S2][S3].
Replaces the general inflation index with a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects spending patterns of people 62 and older, for calculating benefit increases [S2][S3].

Ensures that a benefit increase from the new index is not counted as income when determining Medicaid or SSI eligibility or benefit amounts, so low-income beneficiaries are not penalized for the raise [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and the self-employed would pay Social Security taxes on all their income rather than just the first $176,100, with the share of earnings above the cap taxed at declining rates until the cap disappears after 2031.

drawbacks.text: High earners and the self-employed face a substantially higher combined marginal tax rate as the cap phases out, since the Social Security payroll tax rate (12.4% counting both employer and employee shares) would apply to all wages [S2][S3].

The bill credits surplus earnings in the benefit formula at 3% and 0.25% bend points, so high earners would receive modestly higher benefits in return for their extra taxes, meaning the revenue raised exceeds the new benefit obligations [S3].

The phase-in over six years means the tax increase is gradual, and the bill does not address other Social Security financing questions such as disability insurance trust fund projections beyond the general tax base [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is a more accurate inflation adjustment for seniors and a broader tax base for the program's funding; the main cost is a large tax increase on upper-income earners that begins in 2026 and completes in 2031, with only small incremental benefits returned to those earners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees, and has not received a committee markup or floor vote; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Jill Tokuda introduced the bill on August 12, 2025 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Workforce, and no further action has been recorded [S5].
The bill has 11 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors listed [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet; the bill sits in committee, so the payroll tax cap and current inflation index remain in place for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Current tax cap and benefit formula remain in place

for.name: Rep. Jill Tokuda
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and originally cosponsored it with seven other members

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, no markup scheduled
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has not scheduled action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican cosponsors are listed [S4].

industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax (split between employers and employees, and both halves for the self-employed) on all earnings rather than just the first $176,100, phased in from 2026 to 2031; in return they would accrue modestly higher future benefits under the new surplus-earnings formula.

analysis.trajectory: A payroll tax increase on high earners with no bipartisan cosponsors and no committee action is unlikely to advance in this Congress; the most likely path is that it remains in committee without a markup or vote.
